newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon FTML gets $100 mln syndicated loan.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon FTML gets $100 mln syndicated loan.

text.p: France Telecom Mobile Liban (FTML) will sign on Wednesday a six-year $100 million syndicated loan to help expand its cellular phone network in Lebanon, a Beirut bank that arranged the deal said.

"We are signing tomorrow the syndicated loan in which 19 local and international banks are involved," Nadim Moujaes, Assistant Chairman Advisor of Societe Generale Libano Europeenne de Banque(SGLEB), told Reuters on Tuesday.

The loan was arranged locally by SGLEB while international financing was led by the International Finance Corporation (IFC) -- the private sector arm of the World Bank -- and Societe Generale, France, Moujaes said.
"It is a pioneering success. It is the first deal where local and international syndication is gathered together for a privately-held Lebanese company," he said.
The success reflected the climate of renewed confidence in Lebanon's economy and its future "since it is able to satisfy the exigency of the major finance institutions in the world," Moujaes added.

The loan carries an interest rate of six months LIBOR plus three percentage points. "This is the best interest rate that can be served for a private client in the Lebanese private sector," Moujaes said.
A $75 million portion of the loan was arranged internationally. The IFC put in $30 million and co-arranged with Societe Generale-France the sum of $45 million from 11 international banks.
"Locally, we provided $25 million with the participation of eight local banks," Moujaes said.
FTML has been operating its service in Lebanon under the name Cellis since 1994. Its only rival is the Finnish Libancell, set up in the same year by Finland Telecom and a group of Lebanese investors.
Cellis is operating under a 10-year build, operate and transfer (BOT) deal with the Lebanese government. The deal is renewable in 2004 for two years.

Cellis will use the loan to help finance its $190 million plan to expand the cellular phone network while giving the best possible quality of service over a period of less than five years, Moujaes said.

Both French and Finnish cellular networks have grown rapidly since their introduction in Lebanon. They now have some 200,000 subscribers and rival the fixed-line telephone network which is still being repaired after the 1975-1990 civil war.
"The IFC are very satisfied with FTML's performance and they believe in the future of the communications sector in Lebanon," Moujaes said.
SGLEB is a leading Beirut bank. It has been the fastest growing in terms of credit for the past two years, ranking fifth in terms of credits in 1996 among Lebanon's 82 banks.
